intro.html: Two Latin verbs about the eyes stand behind this whole family. specere means to look (you hear it in inspect and spectator), and videre means to see (you hear it in video and vision). In English the first shows up as spec, spic or spect, and the second as vid or vis.
spec, spic, spect = look. vid, vis = see. Ask where the looking goes: around (circumspect), inward (introspective), back (retrospect), through (perspicacious), ahead (provident).
A root is a clue, not a rule: specious comes from the Latin word for appearance, so a specious claim only looks right. Check every root against the sentence the word sits in.

words.def: careful to think about risks before acting
words.ex: A {circumspect} hiker checks the weather twice before setting out.
words.ctx: Unlike his brother, who signed whatever was put in front of him, Nate was {circumspect}: he read every line of the lease and asked about each fee.
words.etym: From Latin circumspectus, “cautious, well considered,” from circumspicere, “to look around”: circum (around) + specere (to look).

mn.text: Before Pip crosses the busy street, he looks all around: left, right and left again. Looking all around before you act is being {circumspect}.

scene.alt: A boy at a street corner looks left and right before crossing, while a car comes down the road.

words.def: looking inward at your own thoughts and feelings
words.ex: After the game, the {introspective} pitcher sat alone, replaying every choice he had made.
words.ctx: Maya was chatty at parties but {introspective} in her diary, where she asked herself why she felt the way she did and what she wanted to change.
words.etym: From Latin introspicere, “to look into”: intro (inward) + specere (to look).

mn.text: Lila holds a magnifying glass up to her own heart: she is looking inside herself. A person who looks in like that is {introspective}.

scene.alt: A girl sits quietly holding a magnifying glass, thinking about her own feelings.

words.def: a look back at things that have already happened
words.ex: In {retrospect}, packing three sweaters for a beach trip was silly.
words.ctx: At the time, the move to a new town felt like a disaster; in {retrospect}, it was the best thing that ever happened to the family, since it brought them good friends and a better school.
words.etym: From Latin retrospicere, “to look back”: retro (back) + specere (to look).
words.note: Usually heard in the phrase “in retrospect”: looking back now.

mn.cue: RETRO SPECS: glasses that look back
mn.text: Grandpa Gus puts on his old-fashioned specs and pages through photos from fifty years ago. Looking back like that is {retrospect}.

scene.alt: A grandfather in glasses smiles over an old photo album, remembering the past.

words.def: easy to see or notice; standing out
words.ex: Dad’s orange hat made him {conspicuous} in the crowd at the airport.
words.ctx: Lena hoped to slip into class unnoticed, but her bright yellow raincoat made her {conspicuous}, and every head turned when she opened the door.
words.etym: From Latin conspicuus, “in plain sight,” from conspicere, “to look at, notice.”

mn.text: Zoe hides behind a little bush, but her balloons and party hat stick out. “I can spy you!” Ivy calls. Zoe is {conspicuous}.

scene.alt: A girl hides behind a small bush, but her party hat and balloons give her away; her friend points and laughs.

words.def: promising good things to come; favorable
words.ex: A sunny sky on opening day was an {auspicious} start for the new farmers’ market.
words.ctx: The team’s first season began on an {auspicious} note: they won their opening three games, and the coach began to hope for a championship.
words.etym: From Latin auspicium, the reading of signs in the flight of birds, from auspex, “bird watcher”: avis (bird) + specere (to look).

mn.cue: AW, SPECIAL! a rainbow on race day
mn.text: On the morning of the big race, a rainbow arches over the track and Tia gasps, “Aw, special!” A sign that things will go well is {auspicious}.

scene.alt: A runner cheers at a rainbow over the track as a bright bird flies past.

words.def: seeming true or right at first but false underneath
words.ex: The ad’s {specious} promise that the shoes would make anyone run faster fooled no one on the track team.
words.ctx: Dev’s argument sounded convincing at first, but it was {specious}: when his sister checked the numbers, every one of his facts turned out to be wrong.
words.etym: From Latin speciosus, “good-looking, showy,” from species, “appearance,” from specere (to look). It once meant simply “fair to see.”
words.note: Specious (only seeming true) is not spacious (roomy); it comes from species, “appearance.”

mn.text: “See? Shush, don’t check!” says the salesman, because his claim only sounds right until someone looks closely. It is {specious}.

scene.alt: A sly salesman hushes a boy who is inspecting his magic beans sign with a magnifying glass.

words.def: quick to notice and understand things; sharp-minded
words.ex: The {perspicacious} detective noticed that the muddy boots were two sizes too small.
words.ctx: Most readers missed the clue on page ten, but the {perspicacious} few who caught it guessed the ending long before the last chapter.
words.etym: From Latin perspicax, “sharp-sighted,” from perspicere, “to look through”: per (through) + specere (to look).
words.note: Perspicacious describes a sharp mind; perspicuous, a different word, describes writing that is clear.

mn.cue: PURR-SPY-CAT: she sees through it all
mn.text: The Purr-Spy Cat spots the mouse hiding by the boot that everyone else walked right past. A sharp noticer like her is {perspicacious}.

scene.alt: A sharp-eyed cat spots a mouse hiding behind a boot.

words.def: planning wisely for the future, especially by saving
words.ex: The {provident} squirrel buried nuts all autumn and ate well all winter.
words.ctx: Her grandfather had been {provident}, setting aside a little money every month for forty years, so the family did not panic when the factory closed.
words.etym: From Latin providens, “foreseeing,” from providere, “to see ahead, provide for”: pro (ahead) + videre (to see).

mn.cue: PROVIDE-ent: see winter coming, PROVIDE for it
mn.text: The squirrel sees winter coming and provides for it, one basket of food at a time. Seeing ahead and saving is being {provident}.

scene.alt: A busy squirrel fills a basket of food for the winter beside a sign that says for winter.

words.def: to picture something in the mind, especially something that could happen
words.ex: Ada could {envision} the empty lot as a garden full of sunflowers.
words.ctx: Where others saw only a dusty old barn, Rosa could {envision} a bright little theater, and she spent the summer turning that picture into a plan.
words.etym: Made in English in the early 1900s from en- (into) + vision, from Latin videre (to see).

mn.cue: EN-VISION: see it IN your head
mn.text: Before Omar saws a single board, he can see the whole treehouse in his head. To {envision} is to see it in your mind first.

labels.text: EN-VISION: see it IN your mind

scene.alt: A man stands by a tree and a pile of boards, picturing the treehouse he will build.

words.def: a person’s face, or the look on it
words.ex: The old captain’s weathered {visage} broke into a wide grin.
words.ctx: The portrait showed the queen’s stern {visage}, but her letters reveal a warm, funny woman behind that serious face.
words.etym: From Old French visage, “face,” from vis (face), from Latin visus, “a look, sight,” from videre (to see).

mn.cue: VIS-AGE: the face shows your AGE
mn.text: Grandpa’s face in the mirror shows his age: every smile line from eighty happy years. That face is his {visage}.

labels.text: VIS-AGE: the face shows your AGE

scene.alt: An old man with a gray beard smiles at his face in a tall mirror.

after.cap: The prefix tells you which way the eyes are turned.

after.html: Look-alikes: specious (falsely convincing) is not special or spacious. Perspicacious (sharp-minded, said of a person) is not perspicuous (clear, said of writing).

choices: takes up a lot of room
items.why: Specious comes from Latin species, “appearance”: the argument only looks right. It does not mean spacious (roomy) or special.

items.q: Which of these is best described as perspicacious?
choices: a detective who spots a tiny clue
a set of directions that is easy to follow
a window you can see through
items.why: Perspicacious describes a sharp-minded person who notices things. Clear writing is perspicuous, a different word.

items.q: True or false: in retrospect means “looking ahead to the future.”
items.why: False. Retro- means back: in retrospect means looking back at what already happened.

items.q: Both spec and vid mean look or see. Which word means “seeing ahead and planning for it”?
items.why: Pro- means ahead and vid means see: a provident person sees the future coming and saves for it.

items.q: Type the word built on spic (look) that means “easy to see; standing out.”
items.why: Conspicuous: something so plain to the eye that everyone looks at it.
